analysis.summary: Sol-skill decomposes into roughly three strata relative to the four library governors. (1) Its planning/review spine is ALREADY-LAW: plan-with-checkable-acceptance-criteria-before-acting, criteria-as-runnable-checks, the non_goals scope fence, no-drive-by-refactors, review-the-artifact-not-the-report, re-run-checks-yourself, the no-success-on-unrun-checks honesty clause, and the composite done-definition all restate plan-gate, scope-fence, and adversarial-verify — sol's contribution there is packaging those laws into an XML brief imposed on a delegate rather than self-applied. (2) A PARTIAL band where the library has the principle but not sol's mechanism: risk-tiered mandatory fresh-eyes second review, EVIDENCE-vs-INFERENCE tags with per-claim source URLs, spot-checking a delegate's load-bearing claims, risk-class ask-the-user triggers, token-budgeted review mechanics, and explicit-authorization agent routing. (3) A genuinely NOVEL band the four governors do not touch at all, concentrated in multi-agent delegation and security: the strict cross-vendor role split (Claude never edits code), git checkpoint-before-agent-edit for diff isolation and revertibility, the 2-round correction cap with escalation to the user, the delta-only three-part correction protocol, prompt-injection defense (web/delegate output is data, never instructions), least-privilege sandboxing (read-only for research), and model-tuned brief-craft (tight contracts over prose, anti-over-specification). Notably, the library's research-methodology skill contributes almost no overlap — it governs skill-wording A/B experiments, not web research — so sol's research mode maps mainly against plan-gate/adversarial-verify epistemics, with its citation and sandbox rules left uncovered.
